SpaceX IPO occurred on June 12, 2026, marking the largest initial public offering in history with a target valuation of US$1.77 trillion.
SpaceX IPO listed on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol SPCX with a subscription price of US$135 per share.
SpaceX IPO raised approximately US$75 billion through the sale of 555,555,555 Class A shares to the public.
SpaceX IPO allowed Elon Musk to retain 82–85% of voting power through Class B shares despite owning only 42% of the total equity.
SpaceX IPO included a lock-up period of 366 days for Musk and insiders, while other pre-IPO investors faced an 180-day staggered lock-up.
SpaceX IPO secured early inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 index just 15 trading days after listing due to a specific rule change.
SpaceX IPO was underwritten by a syndicate led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley with JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citigroup as other underwriters.
SpaceX IPO faced criticism from analysts who argued the valuation was significantly overvalued compared to independent models suggesting fair values between US$780 billion and US$1.3 trillion.
SpaceX IPO generated massive demand from index funds due to mandatory purchases triggered by its rapid inclusion in major market indices.
SpaceX IPO resulted in a first-day close of US$161 per share, representing a 19% increase and a market capitalization of approximately US$2.1 trillion.
SpaceX IPO included a controversial requirement for underwriting banks to purchase subscriptions to Grok as a condition of their involvement in the deal.
SpaceX IPO was followed by a US$20 billion bond issue launched ten days after listing to repay bridge loans and cover corporate expenses.
SpaceX IPO saw its share price fall below the US$135 IPO price within a month, sliding toward US$123–125 despite initial bullish analyst targets.
SpaceX IPO relied heavily on projected revenue from its xAI subsidiary and compute contracts with Anthropic and Google to justify its astronomical valuation.
SpaceX IPO excluded investors from Hong Kong and China due to concerns regarding critical technology export controls and regulatory risks.
